# `string.split(s, "")` is the characters of s, on every target.
#
# Kotlin's own split is not: `"abc".split("")` answers `["", "a", "b", "c", ""]`
# where Go's strings.Split and JavaScript's String.split both answer
# `["a", "b", "c"]`. The calculator splits its entry into characters to lay
# them out in fixed cells, so on Android it got two cells it never asked for --
# one of them at the front, shifting the whole readout along and pushing the
# last digit off the right-hand edge. Nothing said so; the display was simply
# wrong by one cell.

sngl test --platform none app.sngl
stdout '2 tests, 0 failures'

sngl test --platform bubbletea app.sngl
stdout '2 tests, 0 failures'

# The Kotlin emitter goes through a helper rather than the built-in.
sngl generate --platform android --lang kotlin -o a app.sngl
grep '_snglSplit\(' a/MainScreen.kt
! grep '\.split\(""\)' a/MainScreen.kt

-- app.sngl --
import . "sngl:ui"
import . "sngl:test"

output {
    none { html }
    go { bubbletea }
}

func chars(s string) list<string> {
    return string.split(s, "")
}

component main node {
    var n = chars("abc").length()

    text(value="{n}")
}

func testEmptySeparatorGivesTheCharacters(t Test) {
    var got = chars("abc")
    t.assert(got.length() == 3)
    t.assert(got[0] == "a")
    t.assert(got[2] == "c")
}

// A separator that is actually there splits on it, and an empty string has no
// characters to give.
func testOrdinarySeparatorIsUnchanged(t Test) {
    t.assert(string.split("a,b", ",").length() == 2)
    t.assert(chars("").length() == 0)
}

window {
    main
}
